name: Black Sea Fleet Surface Presence

placement_rationale.text: 350 km is explicitly a composite/representative figure per this asset's own employment_notes — deliberately larger than a 'normal' strategic-rear placement to represent the fleet's forced relocation, not one hull's exact position. It sits closer to zero than the individual Admiral Grigorovich (480 km) and Kilo-class (440 km) entries because it represents the fleet's mixed posture, including units still operating or transiting closer to the line, rather than the single most-relocated asset class; all three stay inside the strategic_rear band. USNI Proceedings and Army Recognition (already in sources) document the Sevastopol-to-Novorossiysk shift this figure represents, directly reflecting doctrine.md §2's finding that local air/sea superiority — not doctrine — sets how close a naval asset can safely operate.

short_role: Representative Black Sea Fleet surface presence, shown at a distance reflecting its forced relocation away from Crimea toward more distant, less exposed basing.
characteristics: Historic main base at Sevastopol became untenable under sustained missile and USV threat
Bulk of surviving surface combatants relocated toward Novorossiysk, further from Ukrainian-controlled coastline
Reduced forward presence has been credited with reopening a functional grain export corridor the fleet had previously threatened
employment_notes: This entry's distance on the map is deliberately larger than a 'normal' strategic-rear asset to represent the fleet's actual behavior: it has been pushed further from the line, not merely stationed at long range by original design. That repositioning is itself the story — a fleet that used to operate close to Crimea now bases further away because it has to.
contrast_vs_traditional: Doctrine reference §2's sharpest finding is that local air/drone superiority — not doctrine or preference — sets how close an asset can operate. The Black Sea Fleet's relocation shows the same logic applied at sea: a fleet with no peer navy to fight was nonetheless pushed back by a mix of shore-based missiles and uncrewed surface vessels, the naval equivalent of the tank being forced from 1.5 km to 7 km when it loses local air control.
